canSAR 2026-an update to the public drug discovery knowledgebase.

canSAR 2026 is an updated version of the world's largest public cancer drug discovery knowledgebase, integrating multidisciplinary data into a navigable knowledge map. The update highlights growth across all data types, improved predictive machine learning algorithms, and expanded AI-driven insight generation for hypothesis generation in translational research.

Artificial intelligence in basic and translational cardiovascular research.

This narrative review surveys how machine learning and deep learning are being applied across cardiovascular research, from medical imaging and computational omics to mechanistic simulation and drug discovery. It emphasizes distinguishing genuine AI contributions from routine bioinformatics and biophysical modeling, and critically assesses study design, independent biological units, validation strategies, and strength of inference in representative studies.

Toll-Like Receptors in Mycoplasma Infections: Immunopathogenesis, Cheminformatics, and Machine Learning-Based Insights into TLR-Targeted Therapeutics.

This review examines how Toll-like receptors recognize Mycoplasma components such as lipoproteins, glycolipids, and CpG-rich DNA, triggering NF-κB and MAPK signaling that can both clear infection and drive chronic inflammation. The authors integrate cheminformatics and machine learning approaches to identify and prioritize potential TLR-targeted therapeutics for Mycoplasma infections. The work highlights the dual protective and pathogenic role of TLR signaling in mycoplasma disease.

AI-powered virtual cells, digital twins and agentic AI are reshaping multi-omics, spatial biology and drug discovery.

This perspective argues that combining single-cell and spatial omics with generative AI is enabling a new class of 'virtual cell' and 'digital twin' models that capture cellular dynamics, spatial context, and adaptive treatment responses rather than static molecular snapshots. The authors frame agentic AI as a key driver of this shift, with implications for multi-omics integration, spatial biology, and drug discovery workflows.

From static structures to conformational ensembles: Artificial intelligence for protein sampling and dynamics.

This review discusses how machine learning and AI are moving beyond static protein structure prediction toward modeling protein conformational ensembles and dynamics. It highlights the challenges posed by the broad timescales of protein motion and the complexity of conformational relationships, and argues that fast, scalable ensemble representations could enable genome-scale studies of protein function with applications in drug discovery and protein engineering.

Machine learning for small-molecule antibiotics - discovery to pre-clinical optimization.

This review examines how machine learning is being applied across the antibiotic development pipeline, from initial small-molecule discovery through pre-clinical optimization, in response to the escalating antimicrobial resistance crisis. It highlights the urgent need for novel antibiotics given the sparse pipeline and frames ML as a tool to accelerate and de-risk discovery amid weak economic incentives for traditional pharma.

BioLM-Score: Language-Prior Conditioned Probabilistic Geometric Potentials for Protein-Ligand Scoring.

The authors introduce BioLM-Score, a protein-ligand scoring method that conditions a probabilistic geometric potential on pretrained biomolecular language-model representations. They test whether these language priors improve scoring over a controlled geometric baseline across affinity prediction, pose selection, and virtual screening. The work probes how pretrained representations can compensate for limited structural coverage in geometric likelihood models.

A Machine Learning-Enhanced Ligand-Based Workflow Identifies Novel Cryptosporidium parvum Inhibitors.

The authors developed a ligand-based virtual screening workflow combining Thompson Sampling, a pharmacophore model, and a machine learning classifier to search 51 million virtual compounds from Enamine's REAL database for new Cryptosporidium parvum inhibitors. This approach identified novel candidate compounds targeting a parasite that currently has only one largely ineffective FDA-approved treatment, addressing an unmet need for cryptosporidiosis therapies.

Learning inhibitor interactions from protein deep mutational scanning data and deep learning models.

This preprint benchmarks protein language models, geometric deep learning, and structure prediction methods on deep mutational scanning data for the MET kinase across 11 inhibitor conditions, testing how well these models generalize to mutation-dependent drug responses. The authors find that small mutational perturbations can produce large effects on drug sensitivity, revealing limits in current models' ability to predict inhibitor interactions beyond their training sets. The work provides a systematic assessment of model generalization for computational drug discovery.

Who Knows Medicinal Chemistry? Expertise, Attrition, and the Dissolving Boundaries of a Craft.

This Viewpoint argues that medicinal chemistry expertise is largely tacit and poorly captured by binary possess-or-lack classifications, especially given high attrition rates in drug design outcomes. The author proposes a more defensible way to measure expertise as disciplinary boundaries dissolve under new modalities, AI, and cross-organizational collaboration.

Democratizing Drug Discovery: A Scalable Open-Source Pipeline for Massive Specific Protein Target QSAR Modeling Using ChEMBL.

The authors present an open-source, automated pipeline that builds QSAR models at scale using ChEMBL data, generating 2263 predictive models across many protein targets with regression and classification approaches. The pipeline combines ErG and RDKit descriptors with Random Forest and XGBoost, using Optuna for hyperparameter tuning and strict quality-control thresholds. This democratizes access to large-scale virtual screening by providing a reproducible, freely available alternative to proprietary AI/ML drug-discovery tools.

Drug Design and Discovery: The Long Road From Hansch Analysis to Artificial Intelligence.

This review traces the historical evolution of QSAR (quantitative structure-activity relationships) from Hansch analysis to modern machine learning and AI approaches in drug discovery. It highlights how changes in molecular representation led to an explosion of descriptors and how big data demanded advanced statistical techniques, culminating in AI as an integral part of pharmaceutical research.

A Hybrid Ligand- and Structure-Based Drug Design Invoked through Square Attention in Protein-Ligand Transformer.

The paper introduces a protein-ligand Transformer model that uses a novel 'square attention' mechanism to jointly evaluate binding affinity and identify the specific amino acid residues and ligand atoms driving interactions. This hybrid ligand- and structure-based approach aims to improve computer-aided drug design by combining affinity prediction with interpretable interaction mapping.

CB-Smart: A Cloud-Based Machine Learning Platform for Screening Cannabinoid Receptor Ligands.

CB-Smart is a cloud-based machine learning platform that predicts whether small molecules bind to the cannabinoid receptors CB1 and CB2 and estimates their relative binding affinity, aiming to replace or accelerate conventional structure-based virtual screening. It was trained on curated experimentally validated cannabinoid ligands together with GPCR decoy molecules, making ligand screening for these drug targets faster and more scalable.

GPCRAgent: an intelligent multi-agent platform integrating knowledge graphs and large language models for GPCR-targeted drug discovery.

GPCRAgent is a multi-agent platform that combines knowledge graphs with large language models to support GPCR-targeted drug discovery. It aims to overcome the limitations of standalone LLMs—insufficient structured domain knowledge and poor interpretability—by integrating curated GPCR knowledge into the reasoning process. The platform is designed to systematically characterize GPCR functions and ligand interactions in silico, reducing reliance on costly experimental approaches.

QRxVision: Multimodal QR Encoding and Computer Vision for Domain-Specific Drug Discovery.

QRxVision introduces a multimodal framework that combines QR-code-like encoding of molecular data with computer vision to enable domain-specific drug discovery. The approach aims to improve high-throughput virtual screening by representing chemical information in a format amenable to image-based deep learning, potentially increasing accuracy and accessibility. The work sits at the intersection of cheminformatics, computer vision, and drug screening.

GAC-BiT-CNN: A Hybrid Generative Adversarial Capsule-Transformer-CNN Model with Fused Protein Language Model Embeddings for Methyltransferase Prediction.

The authors present GAC-BiT-CNN, a hybrid deep learning framework that combines generative adversarial capsule networks, a bidirectional transformer, and a convolutional neural network, using fused protein language model embeddings to predict methyltransferases from sequence. The model is positioned as a computational tool for identifying these epigenetically important enzymes, which are implicated in cancer and neurodegenerative disease. The abstract describes the architecture but does not report benchmark results or comparisons with existing methods.

Prediction of Molecular Physicochemical Properties Using Molecular Structure and Characteristics.

This study addresses the limited generalization of current molecular property predictors under rigorous scaffold splitting by combining molecular descriptors with learned structural representations. The authors propose a hybrid approach that leverages both molecular structure and characteristics to improve prediction of solubility, hydration free energy, and lipophilicity. The work targets drug discovery and materials science applications where accurate physicochemical property prediction is critical.

ML-QSAR and Fragment Selectivity for the Identification of Fourth-Generation EGFRL858R/T790M/C797S Inhibitors.

This study combines machine-learning QSAR models, fragment-level selectivity analysis, large-scale virtual screening of the ZINC database, and MD simulations to identify potential fourth-generation inhibitors targeting the EGFRL858R/T790M/C797S mutant, a key resistance variant in lung cancer. XGBoost models trained on ChEMBL bioactivity data achieved strong predictive accuracy (R² = 0.74–0.81) with interpretable SHAP attributions, and fragment analysis highlighted structural motifs used to guide screening. The workflow yields candidate compounds for further experimental validation.

Computer-Aided Drug Design for Immunosuppressive Tumor Microenvironment Reprogramming: A Critical Review.

This critical review examines how computer-aided drug design (CADD) can be used to identify and test molecular interventions that reprogram the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment in solid tumors. It distinguishes observational AI predictions from actionable molecular hypotheses and discusses the experimental evidence—patient-derived models, spatial and multi-omics profiling, simulation, and pharmacology—needed to validate them.

Emerging Computational Advances in Simulating PCSK9 Variant Dynamics for Therapeutic Design Against Hypercholesterolemia.

This review surveys computational approaches for simulating how PCSK9 variants behave structurally and dynamically, with the goal of informing therapeutic design against hypercholesterolemia. It highlights that clinical translation has focused almost exclusively on the rigid catalytic domain that binds LDLR, while the flexible C-terminal cysteine-rich domain remains underexplored as a drug target. The paper argues that emerging simulation methods could open new avenues for targeting this challenging protein.

HierL2GDTA: Hierarchical Interaction Modeling with Local and Global Features for Drug-Target Affinity Prediction.

HierL2GDTA is a sequence-based deep learning framework that predicts drug-target binding affinity by combining pretrained protein and molecular representations with multi-scale convolutions for local features and bidirectional GRU plus dilated convolutions for broader context. It aims to better integrate ligand and protein representations for interaction modeling than prior methods. The work is an incremental architectural contribution to computational drug discovery.

A Machine-Learning Framework Integrating Frequency-Domain Spectral Features for Ligand Classification and Candidate Prioritization.

The authors introduce THz-FD, a machine-learning framework that fuses conventional molecular descriptors with terahertz frequency-domain spectral features to classify Na+/K+-ATPase ligands and prioritize drug candidates. Using Extra Trees, Random Forest, and SVM classifiers, they show that adding frequency-domain information can improve ligand classification and retrospective ranking. The work suggests that spectral behavior in the THz regime offers complementary molecular information beyond static structural descriptors.

Integrating Artificial Intelligence with High-Throughput Biological Testing for Antimicrobial Drug Discovery.

This review examines how AI models—particularly graph-based and generative approaches—are being combined with high-throughput screening and prospective biological testing to discover new antibacterial compounds. The authors report that these AI-guided strategies have yielded prospectively confirmed active compounds, pathogen-selective candidates, and chemical scaffolds distinct from familiar antibiotics, though the abstract is truncated before full comparative results. Overall, it argues that integrating AI with experimental validation pipelines can help address the dwindling output of conventional antibiotic discovery.

Navigating the Pharma 4.0 revolution: how AI-enabled applications and predictive modelling shaped pharmaceutical development in the post-pandemic era: a systematic review.

Artificial Intelligence as a Multifaceted Toolkit for Antibacterial Drug Discovery against Resistance.

This review argues that AI can be applied as a structured toolkit across the antibacterial drug discovery pipeline to combat antimicrobial resistance, rather than as a single isolated technique. It maps AI capabilities—multi-omics integration, pattern recognition, and predictive modeling—onto different resistance mechanisms and translational stages, from target identification through clinical development. The paper aims to define how AI should be rationally deployed at each stage to address slow antibiotic discovery and limited target diversity.
